title: Why We Forget What We Read
summary: Popular science on memory and study habits — passives, cause and effect, AWL vocabulary.
text:
Most people assume that reading a text twice is a reliable way to learn it. Research on memory suggests the opposite: rereading feels productive precisely because it is easy, and that feeling of ease is often mistaken for understanding.

In a well-known series of experiments, students who reread a passage reported high confidence about how much they had retained. When they were tested a week later, however, they performed no better than students who had read the passage only once. What did make a measurable difference was being asked to recall the content without looking at it.

The explanation is that retrieval is a form of practice. Each time information is pulled out of memory rather than pushed in, the route to it is strengthened. Rereading, by contrast, mostly increases familiarity with the appearance of the words on the page.

This has a practical consequence for language learners. After finishing a text, it is more useful to close the book and try to summarise it aloud — imperfectly, with gaps — than to read it a third time. The discomfort is not a sign that the method is failing. It is the method working.

None of this implies that input does not matter. You cannot retrieve what you never encountered. The point is narrower: exposure creates the raw material, but retrieval is what turns it into something you can use.
